lessons.title: Linked List Fundamentals and Traversal
lessons.description: Understand nodes, references, head pointers and traversal.
lessons.content: A singly linked list consists of nodes, each containing a value and a reference to the next node. The head points to the first node; an empty list has head = None. Unlike an array, a linked list does not support constant-time access by index: reaching position i requires following i links, so lookup is O(n). Traversal is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. A node can be prepended in O(1) time by pointing it to the old head and updating head. In Python, a class is used to represent nodes. Be careful with empty lists, single-node lists, and accidental cycles.

lessons.title: Insertion, Deletion and Search
lessons.content: To insert at the beginning, create a node whose next reference points to the existing head. To insert after a known node, set new.next to current.next before changing current.next; reversing these operations can lose part of the list. To delete the head, return head.next. To delete a node after a known predecessor, change predecessor.next to predecessor.next.next. Searching for a value requires O(n) time in the worst case. If a predecessor is not already known, deletion by value also requires a search. Always decide whether functions mutate the list or return a new head, and test deletion from an empty list and the final remaining node.

lessons.title: Reverse a Singly Linked List
lessons.description: Learn the iterative three-pointer reversal pattern.
lessons.content: Reversing a singly linked list means making every next reference point backward. The iterative solution uses three variables: previous, current and next_node. Save current.next before redirecting it, then advance the pointers. When current becomes None, previous is the new head. The algorithm takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space. A recursive reversal is possible, but it uses O(n) call-stack space. Test empty lists, one node and multiple nodes. Do not confuse changing node links with merely reversing a list of copied values.

examples.title: Reverse a Singly Linked List Example
examples.explanation: Run this example in Python 3 and trace each reference update.
examples.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None):
        self.value, self.next = value, next

def reverse(head):
    previous = None
    current = head
    while current is not None:
        next_node = current.next
        current.next = previous
        previous = current
        current = next_node
    return previous

head = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3)))
head = reverse(head)
while head:
    print(head.value)
    head = head.next

lessons.title: Fast and Slow Pointers
lessons.description: Find middle nodes and detect cycles efficiently.
lessons.content: The fast-and-slow pointer technique advances one pointer by one node and another by two nodes. To find the middle, stop when fast reaches the end; slow then points to the middle (for even lengths, this common version chooses the second middle). Floyd’s cycle detection checks whether fast and slow ever meet. If they meet, a cycle exists; if fast reaches None, the list is acyclic. Both algorithms take O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Always guard access to fast.next by checking fast is not None first. A cyclic list must not be traversed with an unrestricted while-current loop.

lessons.title: Doubly Linked Lists and Interview Patterns
lessons.description: Compare singly and doubly linked lists and combine pointer techniques.
lessons.content: A doubly linked list stores both previous and next references, allowing traversal in either direction. Given a node, deletion can be O(1) because its predecessor is directly available, but the two neighboring links must both be repaired. Doubly linked lists use more memory per node than singly linked lists. Common interview patterns include dummy/sentinel nodes for easier edge-case handling, merging two sorted lists by relinking nodes, and using fast/slow pointers to locate the midpoint. Explain which operations need a head or tail reference, and distinguish O(1) link updates from O(n) searches.

examples.title: Doubly Linked Lists and Interview Patterns Example
examples.explanation: Run this example in Python 3 and trace each reference update.
examples.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

def append(tail, value):
    node = Node(value)
    if tail is not None:
        tail.next = node
        node.prev = tail
    return node

first = Node(1)
last = append(first, 2)
print(first.next.value, last.prev.value)

quizzes.question: What does the head of a singly linked list reference?
quizzes.explanation: The head references the first node, or None for an empty list.

quizzes.question: What is the worst-case time to access the kth node of a singly linked list?
What is the time complexity of prepending a node when the head is known?
quizzes.explanation: Only a constant number of references change.

quizzes.question: Which reference should be saved before reversing current.next?
quizzes.explanation: Save the next node before overwriting the link.

quizzes.question: What is the extra space complexity of iterative linked-list reversal?
quizzes.explanation: Only a fixed number of references are stored.

quizzes.question: What is the usual stopping condition for fast/slow middle finding?
options: fast is None or fast.next is None
quizzes.explanation: The fast pointer stops when it reaches the end.

quizzes.question: What indicates a cycle in Floyd’s algorithm?
options: Fast and slow reference the same node
quizzes.explanation: Meeting at the same node indicates a cycle.

quizzes.question: Which link exists in a doubly linked node but not a typical singly linked node?
quizzes.explanation: Doubly linked nodes also reference their predecessors.

quizzes.question: Why use a dummy node during deletion?
quizzes.explanation: A sentinel gives a consistent predecessor even for the head.

quizzes.question: What is the worst-case time to search for a value in an unsorted linked list?
quizzes.explanation: Potentially every node must be checked.

exercises.title: Build and Traverse a Singly Linked List
exercises.description: Implement a linked list and print its values.
exercises.instructions: Create a Node class and a function to_list(head) returning node values in order. Test an empty list, a single node, and three nodes. Explain O(n) time.

exercises.title: Insert and Delete by Value
exercises.description: Handle link updates and edge cases.
exercises.instructions: Implement prepend(head, value) and delete_first(head, value). Return the new head. Test deleting the first, middle, last and missing values without losing other nodes.

exercises.title: Reverse Linked List In Place
exercises.instructions: Implement reverse_list(head) using O(1) auxiliary space. Test [], [1], and [1,2,3,4]. Do not build a separate list of nodes.

exercises.title: Find Middle Node
exercises.instructions: Implement middle_node(head) returning the second middle for even-length lists. Test lists of length 0 through 6. Explain O(n) time and O(1) space.

exercises.title: Detect a Linked List Cycle
exercises.instructions: Implement has_cycle(head) using O(1) auxiliary space. Create one cyclic and one acyclic test list. Compare node identity, not node values.
